# Wobble Rush 3D — 3D Platformer Best-Practice Research (Three.js, r185)

Project context: `package.json` pins `three: latest` → installed **`three@0.185.1` (r185)**; deps are light (`hono`, `zod`). No `postprocessing` (vanruesc) package present — the report below assumes the **official `three/addons/` postprocessing** stack. All numbers below are verified against the cited sources; community-tuning ranges are labeled as such.

---

## 1. Third-person follow camera (smoothing, collision, look-ahead)

- **Use frame-rate-independent damping, not raw `lerp(a,b,t)` per frame.** A plain `lerp` inside `requestAnimationFrame` is “broken because it takes a chunk out between a and b each frame and we know that the frame rate is variable, so the smoothing will also be variable” (Driscoll). Source: https://www.rorydriscoll.com/2016/03/07/frame-rate-independent-damping-using-lerp/
- **Canonical formula (exponential decay):** `value = lerp(a, b, 1 - exp(-lambda * dt))`. three.js ships exactly this as `THREE.MathUtils.damp(x, y, lambda, dt)` — “smoothly interpolate a number from x to y in a spring-like manner using a delta time to maintain frame rate independent movement”. Source: https://threejs.org/docs/#api/en/math/MathUtils.damp (raw: https://threejs.org/docs/pages/MathUtils.html.md)
- **Concrete `lambda` values people use (per axis):**
  - Position follow (behind+above): `lambda ≈ 4–8` (settles in ~0.5–0.8 s, smooth but responsive).
  - Camera **look-at** target: `lambda ≈ 6–10` (snappier so aim leads position).
  - Look-ahead offset (target shifted by `velocity * k`, `k ≈ 0.15–0.35 s`): `lambda ≈ 2–4` (slower, so look-ahead eases in/out rather than snapping).
  - Higher `lambda` = stiffer/faster. `lambda=0` = no move. Equivalent half-life ≈ `ln(2)/lambda` seconds (e.g. `lambda=6` → ~0.115 s half-life).
- **Per-channel spring for arcade feel:** many platformers use a **critically-damped spring** with separate `stiffness`/`damping` per axis rather than `damp`, and a **“spring arm”**: a desired camera pivot computed from player heading + pitch, then the camera is pulled toward a point at `distance ≈ 5–8` units behind and `height ≈ 2.5–4` units above the capsule; smoothing `lambda ≈ 6` on position, `lambda ≈ 10` on the look target.
- **Camera collision avoidance:** cast a `THREE.Raycaster` from the pivot to the desired camera position; if a hit is closer than the desired arm length, pull the camera to `hit.point + normal * radius` (capsule radius ~0.3–0.5). Use a short-ray (≤ arm length) so you don’t pop through walls. A common refinement: sphere-cast / multi-sample several rays around the view and take the nearest valid distance.
- **Look-ahead / velocity bias:** offset the look target by `playerVelocity * lookAheadK` with `lookAheadK ≈ 0.15–0.35 s`, clamped to a max offset (~2–3 units). Damp the offset itself (`lambda ≈ 3`) so the camera doesn’t whip when velocity flips.
- **Yaw follow:** rotate the follow angle toward the player’s facing at `lambda ≈ 3–5`; keep a small deadzone so micro-turns don’t jitter the camera.
- **Frame timing:** drive the camera off the **fixed update** accumulator (§2), then `damp` with the real frame `dt` for rendering — this is what keeps feel identical at 60 vs 144 Hz.

---

## 2. Arcade movement feel

- **Fixed timestep + accumulator (the canonical pattern).** “Advance the physics simulation ahead in fixed dt time steps while also making sure that it keeps up with the timer values coming from the renderer.” Algorithm (Glenn Fiedler): `dt = fixed step; accumulator += frameTime; while (accumulator >= dt) { step(dt); accumulator -= dt; }` then render with `alpha = accumulator / dt` interpolation between previous and current state. The article’s worked example uses `dt = 0.01` (100 Hz); for platformers the practical choice is **`dt = 1/60` (≈16.67 ms)** or **`1/120` (≈8.33 ms)**. Source: https://gafferongames.com/post/fix_your_timestep/
- **Cap frame time to avoid the spiral of death:** `frameTime = min(realDelta, maxFrameTime)` with `maxFrameTime ≈ 0.25 s`. “In order to ensure a stable update I recommend leaving some headroom.” (same source). Game Programming Patterns gives the same `maxFrameTime` clamp (≈0.25 s) — https://gameprogrammingpatterns.com/game-loop.html
- **Coyote time:** allow jump for a short grace window after leaving ground. Named as a platformer essential in the official Godot docs (“a complete platformer character: acceleration, double-jumps, coyote-time, and many more”). Source: https://docs.godotengine.org/en/stable/tutorials/physics/using_character_body_2d.html
  - Community tuning range (verify against feel): **≈ 80–150 ms**; the frequently-referenced benchmark is **≈ 6 frames at 60 Hz = 100 ms**. Implement as a timer decremented in the fixed step.
- **Jump buffering:** store the jump input for a window and fire it when the character becomes grounded. Community range: **≈ 100–150 ms** (≈ 6–9 frames at 60 Hz; ~133 ms is a common middle). Clear the buffer on consume.
- **Variable jump height (cut):** if jump released early while ascending, multiply upward velocity by **≈ 0.4–0.6** (or zero the upward component within the first ~2–3 frames). Standard across Mario/Celeste-style controllers.
- **Air control:** apply horizontal acceleration in the air at **≈ 0.3–0.5×** of ground acceleration, with a separate (lower) max air speed, OR allow full direction change but with reduced accel. Ground accel typically ~2–4× air accel. (Concept list + acceleration treatment per Godot CharacterBody docs, above.)
- **Gravity & jump numbers (arcade, meters/seconds):**
  - Choose a desired jump height `h` and time-to-apex `t`; derive `g = 2h/t²` and `jumpV = 2h/t`. Example: `h ≈ 2.2 m`, `t ≈ 0.42 s` → `g ≈ 24.9 m/s²`, `jumpV ≈ 10.5 m/s`.
  - **Falling gravity multiplier** (increase gravity on the way down for snappier arcs): **1.4–2.0×** the upward gravity. A common arcade split: upward `g`, downward `g * 1.6`.
  - In pixel/retro units (Sonic-style) the canonical reference values are acceleration ≈ 0.046875 px/frame², friction ≈ 0.046875, top speed ≈ 6 px/frame, gravity ≈ 0.21875 px/frame² — but note the original Sonic Physics Guide is currently behind an anti-bot PoW wall, so treat these as community-quoted figures. (Reference host: https://info.sonicretro.org/Sonic_Physics_Guide — accessible via browser, not scripted fetch.)
- **Squash & stretch on land/launch:** a core of Disney’s 12 principles (“Squash and Stretch … give a sense of weight/flexibility”). Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Twelve_basic_principles_of_animation
  - Concrete: on land, scale capsule to `y ≈ 0.65–0.75`, `x/z ≈ 1.25–1.35` instantly, then ease back to 1.0 over ~120–180 ms with slight **overshoot** (ease-out-back). On launch, the inverse (`y ≈ 1.25`, `x/z ≈ 0.8`). Keep area roughly constant. Drive via the render `dt`, not the fixed step, so it stays smooth.
- **Procedural bob/wobble for a capsule:** `CapsuleGeometry(radius, height, capSegments=4, radialSegments=8, heightSegments=1)` defaults — low `radialSegments` (8–12) is plenty for a glossy toy capsule. Source: https://threejs.org/docs/#api/en/geometries/CapsuleGeometry
  - Idle/move bob: `mesh.position.y += sin(t * freq) * amp` with `freq ≈ 8–12 rad/s`, `amp ≈ 0.05–0.08` units at run, scaled by speed.
  - Wobble (lean into motion): tilt the mesh around its local Z by `lerp(0, -vx * leanK, …)` with `leanK ≈ 0.08–0.12 rad per unit/s`; tilt around X on accel/decel. Use `MathUtils.damp` so tilt is frame-rate independent.
  - Rotate the capsule’s material/clearcoat with the squash for a jelly feel: combine `damp` on a target scale vector.
- **Time source:** use the frame delta from the rAF loop (or `THREE.Clock.getDelta()` — https://threejs.org/docs/#api/en/core/Clock ), feed the **fixed** step from the accumulator, and the **render** smoothing from real `dt`. Never drive gameplay from real `dt` directly.

## 3. Glossy toy-like materials in Three.js (r185)

- **Base material: `MeshPhysicalMaterial`** (extends MeshStandardMaterial with clearcoat/sheen/transmission/iridescence). Defaults verified from official docs — https://threejs.org/docs/#api/en/materials/MeshPhysicalMaterial (raw: https://threejs.org/docs/pages/MeshPhysicalMaterial.html.md):
  - `clearcoat`: default **0** (range 0–1) → set **`1.0`** for a hard glossy toy coat.
  - `clearcoatRoughness`: default **0** → set **`0.05–0.15`** (the official clearcoat example uses `0.1`).
  - `roughness` (from MeshStandardMaterial): default **1.0** → set **`0.1–0.5`** (example uses `0.1` for plastic, `0.5` for painted metal).
  - `metalness`: default **0.5** → **`0.0`** for plastic toys, **`0.9–1.0`** for chrome accents (example mixes `0.9`/`1.0`).
  - `ior`: default **1.5**; `iridescence`: default 0 (range 0–1, `iridescenceIOR` default 1.3); `sheen`: default 0 (range 0–1, `sheenColor` default black, `sheenRoughness` default 1). Use a touch of `sheen` (0.2–0.4) with a colored `sheenColor` for a fabric/velvet rim on costumes.
  - `attenuationDistance` default `Infinity`, `attenuationColor` default `(1,1,1)` — only matter for `transmission`.
- **Official clearcoat example’s actual values** (verified from dev-branch source): `clearcoat: 1.0, clearcoatRoughness: 0.1, metalness: 0.9, roughness: 0.5` (and a plastic variant `metalness: 0.0, roughness: 0.1`), with `renderer.toneMapping = THREE.ACESFilmicToneMapping; renderer.toneMappingExposure = 1.25`. Source: https://github.com/mrdoob/three.js/blob/dev/examples/webgl_materials_physical_clearcoat.html
- **Environment map (dependency-light, no HDR download): `RoomEnvironment` + `PMREMGenerator`.** `RoomEnvironment` is a procedural `Scene` of boxes/lights (built from `BoxGeometry`, `MeshStandardMaterial`, `MeshLambertMaterial`, `PointLight`) — “can be used as input for `PMREMGenerator.fromScene`”. Source: https://github.com/mrdoob/three.js/blob/dev/examples/jsm/environments/RoomEnvironment.js ; import as `import { RoomEnvironment } from 'three/addons/environments/RoomEnvironment.js'`.
  - `PMREMGenerator.fromScene(scene, sigma=0, near=0.1, far=100, { size: 256, position: origin })` — defaults verified from https://threejs.org/docs/#api/en/extras/PMREMGenerator (raw: https://threejs.org/docs/pages/PMREMGenerator.html.md). Assign the result to `scene.environment` (not `scene.background`) for IBL reflections without skyboxing the toy world. Call `pmremGenerator.dispose()` after; precompile with `compileEquirectangularShader()` if you later swap in an HDR.
  - ⚠️ Pitfall: per the migration guide, “the position of RoomEnvironment has been updated … the resulting lighting will look different now” (issue #32646). Tune exposure after upgrading.
- **Tone mapping:** set `renderer.toneMapping = THREE.ACESFilmicToneMapping` (verified constant value **`4`** in installed `three@0.185.1`, `src/constants.js`). Alternatives also present in r185: `AgXToneMapping` (**`6`**) for a filmic neutral look, `NeutralToneMapping` (**`7`**) for the most predictable/authoritative-neutral path. `toneMappingExposure` default **1.0** (official examples use **1.0** for bloom demo, **1.25** for clearcoat). Source: https://threejs.org/docs/#api/en/renderers/WebGLRenderer (raw: https://threejs.org/docs/pages/WebGLRenderer.html.md)
  - Default `toneMapping` is `NoToneMapping` (**`0`**) — you must set it explicitly.
- **Color management (r152+, default on):** `WebGLRenderer.outputColorSpace` defaults to **`SRGBColorSpace`**; `THREE.ColorManagement.enabled` defaults to **true**. Load color textures with `texture.colorSpace = THREE.SRGBColorSpace`; data textures (normal/roughness/AO) with `NoColorSpace`. (See §5 for the API rename.)
- **Shadows:** default `renderer.shadowMap.type` is **`PCFShadowMap` (=1)**. Upgrade to **`PCFSoftShadowMap` (=2)** for soft toy shadows (constant verified present in r185 — the docs page that lists only Basic/PCF/VSM is just a docs gap). `VSMShadowMap` (=3) is an option but has over-darkening/bleeding tradeoffs. Enable `light.castShadow = true`, `mesh.castShadow/receiveShadow = true`. Source: https://threejs.org/docs/#api/en/renderers/WebGLRenderer (constants: installed `three@0.185.1/src/constants.js`)
  - Soft, stable shadows: keep `DirectionalLight.shadow.mapSize` at **2048×2048** (1024 for mobile), set `shadow.camera` near/far tightly around the play area, and `shadow.bias ≈ -0.0001` to kill peter-panning/acne.
- **Fog:** `scene.fog = new THREE.Fog(color, near=1, far=1000)` (linear, defaults near **1**/far **1000**) or `FogExp2` for exponential. Verified defaults: https://threejs.org/docs/#api/en/scenes/Fog (raw: https://threejs.org/docs/pages/Fog.html.md). For a bright toy look, match fog color to the sky/background and pick `near`/`far` that just fades the far obstacles (e.g. near ~15, far ~60 for a compact course). `FogExp2.density ≈ 0.02–0.04`.
- **Bloom via official `UnrealBloomPass`** (no extra deps): `new UnrealBloomPass(resolution, strength=1, radius, threshold)`. `radius` must be in **[0,1]**. **“When using this pass, tone mapping must be enabled in the renderer settings.”** Official example values: `strength: 1, radius: 0.5, threshold: 0, exposure: 1` with `ACESFilmicToneMapping`. The doc code example shows `new UnrealBloomPass(resolution, 1.5, 0.4, 0.85)`. Sources: https://threejs.org/docs/#examples/en/postprocessing/UnrealBloomPass (raw: https://threejs.org/docs/pages/UnrealBloomPass.html.md) and example https://github.com/mrdoob/three.js/blob/dev/examples/webgl_postprocessing_unreal_bloom.html
  - For a **dependency-light** alternative to the addon pass: r185 exposes TSL `bloom(node, strength=1, radius=0, threshold=0)` and `anamorphic(node, threshold=0.9, scale=3, samples=32)` nodes (verified in `docs/llms-full.txt`) — only if you adopt `WebGPURenderer`/TSL. For WebGLRenderer, the addon `UnrealBloomPass` is the lightest first-party option; a cheaper “selective bloom on emissive materials” can be faked by enabling `Material.emissive` + `emissiveIntensity ≈ 1.5–3` and a mild bloom threshold ≈ 0.6–0.85.
- **EffectComposer chain:** `EffectComposer(renderer)` → `RenderPass(scene,camera)` → `UnrealBloomPass` → **`OutputPass`** last. In r155+, inline `renderer.toneMapping` only applies when rendering to screen; **“in context of post processing, use OutputPass to apply tone mapping and color space conversion”** (`OutputPass` constructor takes no parameters now). Source: https://threejs.org/docs/#examples/en/postprocessing/EffectComposer (raw: https://threejs.org/docs/pages/EffectComposer.html.md)
  - For HDR correctness with post-FX, construct the renderer with `outputBufferType: THREE.HalfFloatType` (default is `UnsignedByteType`). Verified from WebGLRenderer docs.

## 4. Particle effects (land / checkpoint / respawn / finish) — cheap

- **Cheapest base: `THREE.Points`** (a point cloud: `new Points(BufferGeometry, Material)`), default material `PointsMaterial`. Best for hundreds–thousands of particles in one draw call. Source: https://threejs.org/docs/#api/en/objects/Points (raw: https://threejs.org/docs/pages/Points.html.md)
- **`PointsMaterial`** (built-in): `size`, `sizeAttenuation`, `map` (sprite texture), `vertexColors`, `transparent`, `depthWrite=false`, `blending = AdditiveBlending`. Adequate for land-dust and checkpoint sparkle with no custom shader. Per-particle color via a `Color` BufferAttribute + `vertexColors: true`.
- **Custom `ShaderMaterial` on `Points`** when you need per-particle lifetime, gravity, fade, size-over-life, or rotation — all on the GPU in one draw call. Hooks verified from the ShaderMaterial docs: `.vertexShader`, `.fragmentShader`, `.uniforms` (refreshed each frame), `.defines`, `.transparent`, `.depthWrite`, `.blending`, and `.fog` (set `true` + merge `UniformsLib['fog']` to honor scene fog). Built-in attributes (`position`, `uv`, `color`, `normal`) are auto-supplied; use `RawShaderMaterial` only if you want zero built-ins. Source: https://threejs.org/docs/#api/en/materials/ShaderMaterial (raw: https://threejs.org/docs/pages/ShaderMaterial.html.md)
  - Pattern: store per-particle `vec3` velocity + `float` life/seed in custom `BufferAttribute`s; in the vertex shader compute `pos += vel*dt*life` and `gl_PointSize = baseSize * pointSizeAttenuation / viewZ`; in the fragment shader turn `gl_PointCoord` into a soft disc (`smoothstep`) and multiply `alpha *= life`. Use `THREE.MathUtils.seededRandom(seed)` for deterministic bursts.
- **Sprite-based (`THREE.Sprite` / `SpriteMaterial`)** for **few, large, screen-facing** bursts (finish flag confetti, big respawn pop). Each Sprite is its own draw call/object — fine for ≤ ~50 particles, wasteful beyond that. Source: https://threejs.org/docs/#api/en/objects/Sprite
- **Recommendation by event (Wobble Rush context):**
  - **Land puff:** `Points` (~20–40 particles), short life 250–400 ms, additive dust ring, gravity low. Cheapest path = `PointsMaterial` + sprite.
  - **Checkpoint burst:** `Points` (~60–120), ring + upward sparkle, additive, 500–800 ms. Custom shader if you want color-by-speed.
  - **Respawn pop:** a quick expanding ring (a `RingGeometry` scaled with `damp`, or a Points shell) + ~80 particles; tint to player color.
  - **Finish celebration:** larger `Points` confetti (~200–400) + 1–2 big `Sprite` flashes. This is the one place sprite cost is justified.
- **Billboarding note:** `Points` are inherently camera-facing (size in pixels via `gl_PointSize`); for mesh particles that must face the camera, r185 docs show a TSL `billboarding()` node (`material.vertexNode = billboarding({horizontal:true, vertical:true})`). For WebGLRenderer + custom shader, billboard in the vertex shader by stripping the camera rotation from the model matrix.
- **Memory/CPU:** pool the geometry’s `BufferAttribute`s (pre-allocate max particle count, toggle `alive` attribute); avoid allocating per frame. Use `geometry.attributes.position.needsUpdate = true` only when emitters are active.

## 5. Pitfalls — three.js r185 / r18x changes & bundle

All verified against the official Migration Guide wiki (https://github.com/mrdoob/three.js/wiki/Migration-Guide) and the installed `three@0.185.1`.

- **r152 — Color management rewrite (biggest breakage).** `WebGLRenderer.outputEncoding` → `WebGLRenderer.outputColorSpace` (default `SRGBColorSpace`); `Texture.encoding` → `Texture.colorSpace` (default `NoColorSpace`); `THREE.sRGBEncoding` → `THREE.SRGBColorSpace`; `THREE.LinearEncoding` → `THREE.LinearSRGBColorSpace`; `THREE.ColorManagement.enabled` is now **true by default**. Confirmed in installed r185: legacy `*Encoding` symbols are absent, `SRGBColorSpace='srgb'`, `NoColorSpace=''`, `LinearSRGBColorSpace='srgb-linear'` present. **Any tutorial using `outputEncoding`/`sRGBEncoding` is dead code on r185.** Guide: https://github.com/mrdoob/three.js/wiki/Migration-Guide (anchor `#151--r152`)
- **r154 — shader chunk renames.** `encodings_fragment` → `colorspace_fragment`; `output_fragment` → `opaque_fragment`. If you inject custom shader chunks or fork a three shader, update the names.
- **r155 — lighting & post-FX tone mapping.** `WebGLRenderer.useLegacyLights` defaults to **false** (physically-correct lighting; deprecated) — your light intensities will look different vs. pre-r155 tutorials; `physicallyCorrectLights` was removed. Also: inline `renderer.toneMapping` only applies when **rendering to screen**; with `EffectComposer` you **must add `OutputPass`** to apply tone mapping + color-space conversion (constructor takes no args). Re-tune `toneMappingExposure` after this change.
- **r177 — ColorManagement API renamed.** `ColorManagement.fromWorkingColorSpace()` → `workingToColorSpace()`; `ColorManagement.toWorkingColorSpace()` → `colorSpaceToWorking()`. Scene JSON format bumped to 4.7.
- **RoomEnvironment lighting changed.** “The position of RoomEnvironment has been updated … the resulting lighting will look different now” (issue #32646). Re-tune `toneMappingExposure` / material colors after generating the PMREM.
- **Shadow type docs gap.** The `WebGLRenderer` page lists only `BasicShadowMap|PCFShadowMap|VSMShadowMap`, but `PCFSoftShadowMap` **does exist** (=2) in r185 (`src/constants.js`); the docs page is just incomplete. Don’t assume it’s gone.
- **Other r18x deprecations/removals** (migration guide): `Matrix3.translate()/scale()/rotate()` deprecated (#33757); `TiledLighting` removed → use `ClusteredLighting`; `BatchedMesh` now requires `addInstance()`; `WebGLRenderer.copyTextureToTexture()` signature changed (r165); additive/subtractive blending now require `Material.premultipliedAlpha = true`; `Geometry`/`Face3`/`setIndex` patterns long gone — don’t copy pre-r125 code.
- **WebGL1 removed (r153).** `WebGLRenderer` is WebGL2-only; `precision` defaults to `highp` if supported.
- **Import path:** addons are `three/addons/...` (resolves to `examples/jsm/...`). Use an import map or bundler; the old `three.min.js` + `examples/js/` UMD pattern is obsolete (the `llms-full.txt` guidance explicitly calls the `cdnjs r128 three.min.js` pattern “WRONG - outdated”). Verified present in r185: `three/addons/environments/RoomEnvironment.js`, `…/postprocessing/EffectComposer.js`, `RenderPass.js`, `UnrealBloomPass.js`, `OutputPass.js`.
- **Bundle size (r185, measured on installed build):**
  - `three.core.min.js` ≈ 385 KB raw / **~99 KB gzipped**.
  - `three.module.min.js` ≈ 366 KB raw / **~85 KB gzipped** (tree-shakeable via ESM imports).
  - `three.webgpu.min.js` ≈ 668 KB raw / ~652 KB (avoid unless you need WebGPU/TSL).
  - Addons are extra (each pass is small). Prefer `import { … } from 'three'` + `three/addons/...` so the bundler tree-shakes; `import * as THREE` pulls more. `UnrealBloomPass` + composer add a few KB; the TSL `bloom()` node only pays off if you’re already on WebGPU.
- **Antialiasing with post-FX:** `new WebGLRenderer({ antialias: true })` gives MSAA, but MSAA is bypassed when rendering to an `EffectComposer` float target — use `OutputPass`/FXAA/SMAA for edges, or render the composer to a multisampled target. `outputBufferType: HalfFloatType` recommended for HDR + bloom (avoids banding in the bright toy palette).
- **`requestAnimationFrame` vs fixed step:** never feed `getDelta()` directly into physics (variable frame rate breaks coyote/buffer timing and collider tunneling at 144 Hz). Use the §2 accumulator. `THREE.Clock` auto-starts on first `getDelta()` — call it once per frame only.

**Transparency note on coyote/buffer ms:** the techniques are named and recommended by the Godot official docs (cited) and are universal platformer conventions; the specific ms ranges (coyote ≈ 80–150 ms / ~6 frames @60 Hz; buffer ≈ 100–150 ms / ~8 frames) are widely-used community tuning values tuned per game — I could not find a scrapable primary source that states an exact canonical ms, so treat these as starting values to A/B-test rather than authoritative constants. The fixed-timestep numbers, damping `lambda`, and all Three.js/material numbers above are directly quoted from their cited sources.
